note: 今晩 'konban' (this evening) + the topic particle は, the opening of an unfinished sentence, just like こんにちは. The final は is the particle, so it is written は but said 'wa'.
お (honorific) + 休み 'yasumi' (rest) + なさい, a polite imperative. Said when going to bed or parting late at night. Family and friends shorten it to おやすみ.
From 初めて 'hajimete' (for the first time) in a polite te-form. Opens a self-introduction; it is normally followed by your name and よろしくお願いします.

example.target: はじめまして、田中です。
example.en: Nice to meet you, I am Tanaka.

en: Please treat me well / I look forward to working with you
target: よろしくお願いします
note: よろしく is the adverb form of 宜しい 'yoroshii' (good, fine), お願いします is 'I humbly request'. No English equivalent; it closes introductions and any request for cooperation.

literal: how could I have done (anything worth thanks)?
note: どう (how) + いたしまして, the humble form of する (to do). It politely denies that your help was any trouble. In casual speech people often just say いえいえ (no, no).
御免 'gomen' is ご (honorific) + 免 (exemption, pardon); なさい is a polite command. Warmer and more personal than すみません; ごめん alone is for friends.

example.target: 遅れてごめんなさい。

en: Excuse me (entering or leaving a room)
note: 失 (lose) + 礼 (courtesy): 'I am about to be impolite'. Said when entering a superior's office, hanging up the phone, or leaving. Past form 失礼しました apologizes for something already done.
お (honorific) + 願い 'negai' (wish, request) + します. Use it when asking for a thing or a service: コーヒーをお願いします. Not for 'please go ahead', which is どうぞ.

example.target: 水をお願いします。

en: Thank you for the meal (after eating)
note: ご (honorific) + 馳走 'chisō' (literally 'run about', the host rushing around to gather food) + 様 (respectful title). The partner of いただきます; said to the cook or when leaving a restaurant.
Short for ただいま帰りました 'I have just now returned'. Called out when you come through the door; the reply is おかえりなさい. ただ今 is also a formal word for 'right now'.
お + 帰り 'kaeri' (returning) + なさい. Answer to ただいま. Also used by shops and hotels: 'welcome back'. Friends say just おかえり.
行って 'itte' (going) + 来ます 'kimasu' (I come). Said when leaving the house or office; promises a return. The household answers いってらっしゃい.

en: Take care, see you later (to someone leaving)
note: 行って + いらっしゃい, the honorific imperative of 'come'. Reply to いってきます. Flight attendants and hotel staff also use it to send guests off.
元気 'genki' = 元 (origin) + 気 (spirit, energy). Not an everyday opener like English 'how are you'; it is for people you have not seen for a while. Answer: はい、元気です.

example.target: お久しぶりです。お元気ですか。
example.en: Long time no see. How are you?

note: Also means 'here you are', 'present' (at roll call) and 'I am listening'. In conversation はい often signals attention, not agreement. Casual form: うん 'un'.
Polite 'no'; casual ううん 'uun'. Japanese often avoid a flat いいえ and soften refusals with ちょっと (it is a bit...) or 大丈夫です. Also used to mean 'not at all' after thanks.

en: Excuse me for intruding (entering someone's home)
note: 邪魔 'jama' = 邪 (evil) + 魔 (demon), a Buddhist term for an obstacle to practice, now simply 'nuisance'. Said at the door when visiting; お邪魔しました when leaving.
また 'mata' (again) + 明日 'ashita' (tomorrow). Pattern: また + time word: また来週 (see you next week), またね (see you). Lighter than さようなら.
じゃあ is a contraction of では 'de wa' (well then), ね seeks agreement. The everyday goodbye among friends; the polite version is では、また (well, until next time).

target: おめでとうございます
note: From めでたい 'medetai' (auspicious, happy) with the honorific お and polite ございます. Put the occasion first: お誕生日おめでとう (happy birthday), 明けましておめでとう (happy new year).

example.target: ご結婚おめでとうございます。

note: 大 (big) + 丈夫 'jōbu' (sturdy, robust; in classical Chinese a 'great man'). Na-adjective. Means 'fine, safe, OK' and, as 大丈夫です, is a polite way to decline: 'no thanks, I'm fine'.

example.target: 大丈夫ですか。

en: Excuse me for leaving before you
note: お先に 'osaki ni' (ahead, before you) + 失礼します. The standard phrase when leaving the office while colleagues are still working; they answer お疲れ様でした.
Polite command form of いらっしゃる, the honorific verb for 'come, go, be'. Shouted by staff in every shop and restaurant. No reply is expected from the customer.
Offers or permits: handing something over, letting someone go first, inviting them to sit. Pairs with どうも as the reply. Compare お願いします, which asks for something.

example.target: どうぞ、お入りください。

note: An adverb meaning 'very much' that stands in for the phrases it once intensified: どうもありがとう (thanks a lot), どうもすみません. On its own it is a casual thanks, greeting or acknowledgement.
Sino-Japanese (on) reading いち. The native reading appears in 一つ 'hitotsu' and 一人 'hitori'. One horizontal stroke; the simplest kanji in the language.
On reading に, as in 二月 'nigatsu' (February). Native reading ふた in 二つ 'futatsu' and 二人 'futari' (two people).
さん. Before some counters the following consonant changes: 三本 'sanbon', 三百 'sanbyaku', 三千 'sanzen'. Native reading み in 三つ 'mittsu'.
Two readings: よん and し. し sounds like 死 (death), so it is avoided: hospitals skip room 4, and 四人 (four people) is 'yonin'. But 四月 (April) is 'shigatsu'.
ご. Native reading いつ in 五つ 'itsutsu'. 五月 'gogatsu' is May.
ろく. Often contracts before k/p/h: 六百 'roppyaku' (600), 六本 'roppon', 六回 'rokkai'. Native reading む in 六つ 'muttsu'.
Two readings: なな and しち. しち is easily confused with いち (one) on the phone, so なな is preferred in prices and phone numbers; months use しち: 七月 'shichigatsu' (July).
はち. Contracts to はっ before some counters: 八百 'happyaku' (800), 八千 'hassen', 八分 'happun'. Native reading や in 八つ 'yattsu' and 八百屋 'yaoya' (greengrocer).
Two readings: きゅう and く. く sounds like 苦 (suffering), so きゅう is usual; 九月 (September) is 'kugatsu' though, and 九時 (nine o'clock) is 'kuji'.
じゅう. The native reading is とお 'tō', the only native number without つ. 11 is 十一 'jūichi', 20 is 二十 'nijū': Japanese builds all numbers by stacking these digits.
The native Japanese number series ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ... counts objects of any kind without a counter. Also used for a child's age: 一つ = one year old. Written with the suffix つ.

example.target: りんごを一つください。

note: ふたつ. The same root ふた appears in 二人 'futari' (two people) and 二日 'futsuka' (the 2nd of the month).
みっつ, with a small っ doubling the t. Compare 三日 'mikka' (the 3rd). Ordering in a restaurant: 三つお願いします.
よっつ. The native よ root gives よん, the safe reading of 四 that avoids し (death).
いつつ. Do not confuse with いつ 'itsu' (when). 五日 'itsuka' is the 5th of the month.
むっつ. Root む, also in 六日 'muika' (the 6th).
ななつ. The native root なな is why 'nana' is the everyday reading of 七.
やっつ. Root や; 八百 'yao' in 八百屋 (greengrocer) means 'a great many', not exactly 800.
ここのつ. The longest of the native numbers; 九日 'kokonoka' is the 9th of the month.
ひゃく. Sound changes: 三百 'sanbyaku', 六百 'roppyaku', 八百 'happyaku'. 'One hundred' is simply 百, not 一百.
せん. 三千 'sanzen', 八千 'hassen'. 'One thousand' is just 千. A 千円 'sen'en' note is the smallest Japanese banknote.

example.target: これは千円です。

note: まん. Japanese counts in units of 10,000, not 1,000: 一万 'ichiman' (here 一 is required), 十万 'jūman' = 100,000, 百万 'hyakuman' = a million. A 一万円 note is the largest banknote.

en: counter for long thin things (bottles, pens, trains)
note: The kanji 本 means 'book' or 'origin' on its own; as a counter it counts cylinders: bottles, pens, umbrellas, trains, even films and phone calls. Sound changes: 一本 'ippon', 二本 'nihon', 三本 'sanbon'.

example.target: ビールを二本ください。

en: counter for flat things (paper, tickets, shirts)
note: まい counts sheets, tickets, plates, shirts, pizzas: anything flat. Regular: 一枚 'ichimai', 二枚 'nimai', 三枚 'sanmai'. 何枚 'nanmai' = how many sheets?

example.target: 切符を一枚お願いします。

note: こ counts eggs, apples, pieces of anything compact. Contracts: 一個 'ikko', 六個 'rokko', 八個 'hakko', 十個 'jukko'. The native 一つ series can replace it in casual speech.
両 (both) + 親 'oya' (parent). Used for your own parents; for someone else's say ご両親 'go-ryōshin' with the honorific prefix.
お + 父 'tō' + さん. Use for someone else's parents, or to call your own ('Dad!'). When telling outsiders about your own parents, switch to the humble 父 and 母.

example.target: お母さんは元気ですか。

note: The plain, humble words for your own parents when speaking to people outside the family: 父は医者です. The kanji 父 and 母 are read とう and かあ inside お父さん and お母さん.
Japanese has separate words for older and younger siblings. 兄 'ani' and 姉 'ane' are humble forms for your own; with さん they become お兄さん and お姉さん.
弟 'otōto' and 妹 'imōto'. For someone else's: 弟さん, 妹さん. Younger siblings are addressed by name, never by these words. 兄弟 'kyōdai' means siblings in general.

example.target: 妹は高校生です。
example.en: My younger sister is a high-school student.

en: older brother / older sister (polite, or addressing them)
note: Also how you address a young man or woman you do not know (a waiter, a shop assistant), as English once used 'miss'. Casual family form: お兄ちゃん, お姉ちゃん.
子 'ko' (child) + 供 'domo', an old plural suffix, so 'children' is the original sense; today it is singular or plural. Often written 子ども in schools, avoiding 供 (which also means 'attendant').

example.target: 子供が二人います。

note: 息子 'musuko' and 娘 'musume' are for your own children. For someone else's: 息子さん, 娘さん (or お嬢さん 'ojōsan' for a daughter). 娘 is also 'young woman'.
Note the long vowel: おじいさん 'ojīsan' is grandfather, おじさん 'ojisan' is uncle. Same for おばあさん (grandmother) vs おばさん (aunt). Also means any elderly man or woman.
祖 (ancestor) + 父 (father) / 母 (mother). Formal words for your own grandparents; at home you call them おじいちゃん, おばあちゃん.
夫 'otto' and 妻 'tsuma' are the neutral words for your own spouse. Older alternatives: 主人 'shujin' (master) for husband, 家内 'kanai' (inside the house) for wife, both now felt as dated.
奥 'oku' means the inner part of a house, where the lady of the house traditionally stayed. For someone else's husband say ご主人 'goshujin' (honorable master).
彼女 'kanojo' adds 女 (woman) to 彼. Both also mean boyfriend/girlfriend: 彼女がいます = I have a girlfriend. Japanese usually prefers a name + さん over pronouns.

example.target: 彼は学生です。

note: 友 'tomo' (friend) + 達 'tachi', the plural suffix seen in 私達 'watashitachi' (we). Despite the plural suffix it means one friend or several. 友人 'yūjin' is the formal word.
Kun reading ひと; on readings じん and にん: 日本人 'nihonjin' (Japanese person), 三人 'sannin' (three people). The kanji is said to picture a person standing.
男 'otoko' (male) + の + 人. Bare 男 and 女 can sound blunt, so 男の人 and 女の人 are the polite everyday words; 男性 'dansei' and 女性 'josei' are more formal.
男の子 'otoko no ko' and 女の子 'onna no ko'. 女の子 is used well into adulthood for young women, much like 'girl' in English.
赤 'aka' (red), for a newborn's flushed skin, + ちゃん, the affectionate diminutive of さん. The formal word is 赤ん坊 'akanbō'.
大 (big) + 人 (person), but read おとな, a special reading that ignores the usual readings of both kanji. Tickets are often priced 大人 / 子供.
One and two people are irregular natives: 一人 'hitori', 二人 'futari'. From three on it is Sino-Japanese: 三人 'sannin', 四人 'yonin', 何人 'nannin' (how many people?).

example.target: 三人です。

note: 名 (name) + 前 (front). Asking politely: お名前は? Japanese names put the family name first: 田中花子 'Tanaka Hanako'.

example.target: お名前は何ですか。

note: 先 (before) + 生 (birth). A title of respect for teachers, doctors, lawyers and artists; attach it to a surname like さん. Never call yourself 先生.
皆 'mina' (all) + さん. The polite way to address a group: 皆さん、こんにちは. Without さん, 皆 'minna' is casual.

en: uncle / aunt (also any middle-aged man or woman)
note: Short vowel: おじさん (uncle) vs おじいさん (grandfather). Kids use it for any grown man, and women use おばさん for any middle-aged woman, so take care with the tone.
Very casual male 'I', used among friends and family; rude in formal settings. Women use あたし in the same casual register. 僕 is the softer male choice, 私 is neutral.
ご (honorific) + 飯 'han' (cooked rice). Rice and 'meal' are the same word: 朝ご飯 breakfast, 昼ご飯 lunch, 晩ご飯 dinner. Uncooked rice is 米 'kome'.
From Portuguese 'pão', brought by missionaries in the 16th century, which is why it is not 'bread'. A bakery is パン屋 'pan'ya'. Katakana marks it as a loanword.
Kun reading みず; on reading すい in 水曜日 (Wednesday). 水 means cold water; hot water is a different word, お湯 'oyu'. In a restaurant ask for お水.

example.target: お水をください。

note: The honorific お is almost always attached. Plain お茶 means Japanese green tea; English 'tea' came via the same Chinese word. お茶する 'ocha suru' = to go for a coffee or tea.
From Dutch 'koffie', which explains the 'hī' rather than 'fī'. The old kanji spelling 珈琲 still appears on café signs.
牛 (cow) + 乳 (milk). The loanword ミルク 'miruku' is also common, especially for milk in coffee. 'A cow' on its own is 牛 'ushi'.
Prefix the animal: 牛肉 'gyūniku' (beef), 豚肉 'butaniku' (pork), 鶏肉 'toriniku' (chicken). The radical 月 in 肉-related kanji like 腕 (arm) is actually a squashed 肉.
さかな originally meant 'side dish with sake' (酒菜); the sense narrowed to fish. The kanji is a pictograph of a fish; the radical 魚 appears in names of fish like 鮭 (salmon).
野 (field) + 菜 (greens, vegetable). 菜 also appears in 菜の花 (rapeseed blossom).

example.target: 野菜をたくさん食べます。

note: 果 (fruit) + 物 'mono' (thing), with a special reading くだ. Japanese fruit is often sold as gifts; a perfect melon can cost thousands of yen.
Also written 玉子 (jewel child) on menus, for cooked eggs. 卵焼き 'tamagoyaki' is the rolled omelette served at breakfast and in bento.
寿司 is ateji: kanji chosen for sound, not meaning. The word comes from an old adjective meaning 'sour', because the original dish was fish preserved in fermented rice. Polite: お寿司.
Chinese-style wheat noodles in broth, borrowed from Chinese (拉麺, 'pulled noodles') in the early 20th century, hence katakana. Instant ramen was invented in Japan in 1958.
味噌 'miso' (fermented soybean paste) + 汁 'shiru' (broth, juice). Part of a traditional breakfast with rice. Often called お味噌汁.
酒 'sake' means any alcoholic drink; what English calls sake is 日本酒 'nihonshu' (Japanese liquor). 酒 is read しゅ in compounds. お酒を飲みますか = Do you drink?

example.target: お酒は飲みません。

note: From Dutch 'bier', an Edo-period borrowing. Do not confuse with ビル 'biru' (building, short vowel). 生ビール 'nama bīru' is draft beer.
砂 (sand) + 糖 (sugar), describing its grains. Sounds like the common surname 佐藤 'Satō', a favorite pun.
しお. 塩味 'shioaji' is salt flavor (one of the ramen types). A pinch of salt is scattered for purification at sumo matches and shop doorways.
醤 (fermented sauce) + 油 (oil). English 'soy' comes from this word, via Dutch traders. Pour it into the small dish, not over the rice.
A single-portion meal of rice and side dishes in a box, from home or a shop. Station ones are 駅弁 'ekiben'. Usually said with the honorific: お弁当.
From 握る 'nigiru' (to grip): rice pressed by hand into a triangle, often wrapped in seaweed. Also called おむすび. Every convenience store sells them.
Usually in hiragana; the kanji 林檎 is rare. Aomori prefecture grows most of Japan's apples. りんごジュース = apple juice.
朝 'asa' (morning) + ご飯. Lunch is 昼ご飯 'hirugohan', dinner 晩ご飯 'bangohan'. The formal Sino-Japanese words are 朝食, 昼食, 夕食.

example.target: 朝ご飯は何を食べましたか。
example.roman: Asagohan wa nani o tabemashita ka.
example.en: What did you have for breakfast?

note: U-verb. Also used for taking medicine (薬を飲む) and for soup (スープを飲む). The invitation 飲みに行こう means going out for drinks.

example.target: コーヒーを飲みます。

note: I-adjective, usually written おいしい; the kanji 美味 mean 'beautiful taste'. Men often say うまい 'umai' instead. Negative: 美味しくない; past: 美味しかった.

example.target: このラーメンは美味しいです。

note: From French 'restaurant', borrowed in the Meiji era, so the final 'n' is kept. Used mainly for Western-style places; a cheap canteen is 食堂 'shokudō'.
English 'menu' in katakana. Many restaurants display plastic food models (食品サンプル) in the window, so you can point. Ask: メニューをお願いします.
注文 'chūmon' (an order) + する; irregular suru-verb. Staff ask ご注文は? 'your order?'. Casual verb: 頼む 'tanomu'.

example.target: もう注文しましたか。

note: 会計 'kaikei' = 会 (meet) + 計 (count), 'accounting'. お会計お願いします asks for the bill. You usually pay at the register near the door, not at the table.

example.target: お会計お願いします。

note: 定 (fixed) + 食 (meal). A main dish with rice, miso soup and pickles at a set price. Restaurants serving them are 定食屋 'teishokuya'.
Famous pitch-accent pair: 箸 'HAshi' (high-low) is chopsticks, 橋 'haSHI' (low-high) is bridge. Never stick chopsticks upright in rice; that is done at funerals.
English 'fork'. The same katakana also spells 'folk' (フォークソング, folk song). Spoon is スプーン, knife is ナイフ.
From Dutch 'kop' (or Portuguese 'copo'), an old loan. A coffee cup with a handle is カップ 'kappu' from English; a wine glass is グラス.
From 勧める 'susumeru' (to recommend). お勧めは何ですか 'what do you recommend?' is the most useful question in any restaurant. Also written おすすめ.

example.target: お勧めは何ですか。

note: Verb stem 飲み 'nomi' + 物 'mono' (thing). The same pattern gives 食べ物 (food), 読み物 (reading matter), 買い物 (shopping). お飲み物は? = anything to drink?
食べ (eat) + 物 (thing). 好きな食べ物は何ですか 'what food do you like?' is a classic small-talk question.
English 'dessert'. Beware デザート vs 砂漠 'sabaku' (desert); and スイーツ 'suītsu' (sweets) is the trendier word on café menus.
English 'cake'. Japanese 'Christmas cake' is a strawberry sponge; ショートケーキ 'shōtokēki' means that sponge cake, not shortcake. Counter: 一個 or 一切れ (one slice).
紅 (crimson) + 茶 (tea): named after the color of the brew, while English names it after the leaf. Plain お茶 means green tea, so ask for 紅茶 if you want Western-style tea.
居 (stay) + 酒 (sake) + 屋 (shop): a sake shop where you stay to drink. Dishes are small and shared; a cover charge (お通し 'otōshi') is usual.
喫 (drink, consume) + 茶 (tea) + 店 (shop). The old-style Japanese café with thick toast and siphon coffee; カフェ 'kafe' is the modern word.
店 (shop) + 員 (member). To call staff, say すみません rather than any word for waiter. The apostrophe in ten'in shows ん + い, not the syllable に.
On reading せき. 禁煙席 non-smoking seat, 窓側の席 window seat, 予約席 reserved. Staff may ask お席はお決まりですか.
禁 (prohibit) + 煙 (smoke). Also 'quitting smoking': 禁煙する. The opposite sign is 喫煙 'kitsuen' (smoking allowed).
持ち 'mochi' (carry) + 帰り 'kaeri' (return home). Staff ask 店内でお召し上がりですか、お持ち帰りですか (eat in or take out?). Also テイクアウト.
これ (this) + を (object marker) + ください (please give). Point at the menu and say it. For 'that', use それ (near you) or あれ (over there).
乾 (dry) + 杯 (cup), same idea as 'bottoms up'. Everyone waits for the toast before drinking. Glasses are often clinked lower than the senior person's.
お腹 'onaka' (belly) + が + すいた, past of 空く 'suku' (to become empty). Polite: お腹がすきました. Thirsty is 喉が渇いた 'nodo ga kawaita' (my throat has dried).
I-adjective. Also 'salty' in western Japan. The same kanji read つらい 'tsurai' means 'painful, hard', so context decides. 甘口 'amakuchi' / 辛口 'karakuchi' = mild / hot on curry labels.

example.target: このカレーは辛いですね。
example.roman: Kono karē wa karai desu ne.
example.en: This curry is spicy, isn't it?

note: I-adjective. Beyond taste it means 'lenient, naive' (甘い考え, a naive idea). 甘いもの 'amai mono' is the general word for sweets.
旅 (journey) + 行 (go). 旅行する = to travel; 海外旅行 'kaigai ryokō' = overseas trip. The native word 旅 'tabi' is more poetic.

example.target: 来月、京都へ旅行します。
example.en: Next month I am travelling to Kyoto.

note: Kun reading みぎ; on reading う in 左右 'sayū' (left and right). 右に曲がってください = please turn right. The kanji has a 口 (mouth) under a hand.
ひだり. Looks like 右 but with 工 instead of 口 underneath. Japan drives on the left, so 左側 'hidarigawa' (left side) is where cars go.

example.target: 次の角を左に曲がってください。
example.roman: Tsugi no kado o hidari ni magatte kudasai.
example.en: Turn left at the next corner.

note: Usually in kana (kanji 真っ直ぐ). まっすぐ行ってください = go straight. Also 'honest, direct' about a person.
みち; on reading どう in 道路 (road), 北海道 (Hokkaidō) and the arts: 柔道 'jūdō', 茶道 'sadō' (the 'way' of tea). 道に迷う = to get lost.
地 (land, earth) + 図 (diagram). 地図アプリ = map app. Japanese addresses number blocks, not streets, so a map is essential.
English 'hotel' in katakana. A Japanese-style inn is a 旅館 'ryokan'; a ビジネスホテル is a cheap, compact city hotel.
観 (observe) + 光 (light, glory), from a Chinese classic about 'viewing the glory of a land'. 観光客 'kankōkyaku' = tourist, 観光地 = tourist spot.
English 'passport'. The official word is 旅券 'ryoken' (travel ticket), seen on forms. Hotels may ask to copy it.
荷 (load, cargo) + 物 (thing). Luggage-forwarding services (宅急便) send bags ahead to your next hotel. 手荷物 'tenimotsu' = hand baggage.
交差 'kōsa' (crossing) + 点 (point). Directions usually run: 交差点を渡って、右に曲がる (cross the intersection, turn right).
かど. The same kanji read つの means an animal's horn and read かく means 'angle' (三角, triangle). 角を曲がる = turn the corner.
信 (signal, trust) + 号 (sign, number). A green light is 青信号 'ao shingō' (blue light), because 青 historically covered green.

example.target: 信号を渡ってください。

note: I-adjective; note the long vowel とおい, written with お not う. 遠く 'tōku' = far away (noun/adverb). The opposite is 近い.
I-adjective. 駅から近いです = it is near the station. 近く 'chikaku' = nearby: この近くに銀行はありますか (is there a bank near here?).

example.target: ホテルは駅から近いですか。
example.roman: Hoteru wa eki kara chikai desu ka.
example.en: Is the hotel near the station?

note: U-verb; the place you turn at takes を: 角を曲がる. Also 'to bend, be crooked'. The transitive partner 曲げる 'mageru' = to bend something.
U-verb. 橋を渡る = cross a bridge. Transitive 渡す 'watasu' = to hand over. The kanji appears in 渡航 (overseas travel).
U-verb. 道に迷う = to lose one's way; also 'to be unable to decide' (迷っています, I'm torn). 迷子 'maigo' = lost child.

example.target: 道に迷いました。

note: U-verb; the destination takes に: 駅に着く. The same kanji read 着る 'kiru' means 'to wear'. Formal equivalent: 到着する 'tōchaku suru'.

example.target: 何時に着きますか。

note: 出 (go out) + 発 (depart). 出発する = to depart. Its partner is 到着 'tōchaku' (arrival); both appear on airport boards.
きた; on reading ほく/ほっ in 北海道 'Hokkaidō' and 東北 'Tōhoku'. Station exits are often named by direction: 北口 'kitaguchi' (north exit).
みなみ; on reading なん in 南米 'Nanbei' (South America). 南口 = south exit.
ひがし; on reading とう in 東京 'Tōkyō' (eastern capital). The kanji shows the sun 日 rising behind a tree 木.
にし; on reading せい/さい in 西洋 'seiyō' (the West) and 関西 'Kansai' (the Osaka-Kyoto region).
温 (warm) + 泉 (spring). Volcanic Japan has thousands; you wash thoroughly before entering, and tattoos may be refused. The map symbol ♨ is a Japanese invention.
電 (electricity) + 車 (vehicle). The everyday word for any train; 列車 'ressha' is formal. 電車で行きます = I go by train (で marks the means).

example.target: 電車で会社に行きます。
example.en: I go to work by train.

note: えき. The left part 馬 is 'horse': stations were once post-horse stops. Attach to a name: 東京駅 'Tōkyō-eki'. 駅員 'ekiin' = station staff.
English 'bus'; the same katakana also spells 'bath' (バスルーム). バス停 'basutei' = bus stop. On many buses you board at the back and pay at the front when getting off.
English 'taxi'. Rear doors open and close automatically; do not touch them. タクシーを呼ぶ = to call a taxi.
自 (self) + 転 (turn, roll) + 車 (vehicle): a vehicle you turn yourself. Casual slang: チャリ 'chari'. 自転車に乗る = to ride a bike.
Kun reading くるま; the kanji pictures a cart seen from above. On reading しゃ in 電車, 自転車, 駐車場. 車で = by car.
地下 'chika' (underground) + 鉄 (iron, short for 鉄道 railway). Tokyo has two subway networks, Tokyo Metro and Toei.
新 (new) + 幹 (trunk) + 線 (line). Opened in 1964 for the Tokyo Olympics. Seats come as 自由席 (unreserved) and 指定席 (reserved).
飛行 'hikō' (flight) + 機 (machine). 飛行機で = by plane. The verb is 飛ぶ 'tobu' (to fly).
空 (sky) + 港 'minato' (harbor). 成田空港 'Narita kūkō', 羽田空港 'Haneda kūkō'. The kanji 空 also reads そら (sky) and から (empty).
切 (cut) + 符 (tally, tag). Train and bus tickets; a cinema or concert ticket is チケット. Most locals use an IC card (Suica, Pasmo) instead.

example.target: 切符はどこで買えますか。
example.roman: Kippu wa doko de kaemasu ka.
example.en: Where can I buy a ticket?

note: 乗り 'nori' (riding) + 換え 'kae' (change). Verb: 乗り換える 'norikaeru'. Apps called 乗換案内 (transfer guide) plan every connection to the minute.
U-verb; the vehicle takes に, not を: バスに乗る. Also 'to go along with' (話に乗る). Transitive 乗せる 'noseru' = to give a ride.

example.target: ここでバスに乗ります。
example.en: I get on the bus here.

note: Ru-verb; the vehicle takes を: 電車を降りる. The same reading written 下りる means 'to go down (stairs)'. The kanji 降 also means 'to fall' (rain, snow).

example.target: 次の駅で降ります。
example.en: I get off at the next station.

note: 運転 'unten' = 運 (carry, transport) + 転 (turn, roll); irregular suru-verb. 運転手 'untenshu' = driver, 運転免許 = driving licence.
U-verb. 歩いて 'aruite' (on foot) answers 'how do you get there?'. On reading ほ in 散歩 'sanpo' (a stroll) and 歩道 'hodō' (pavement).

example.target: 駅まで歩いて十分です。
example.en: It is ten minutes on foot to the station.

note: ふね; on reading せん in 船長 'senchō' (captain). The radical 舟 (boat) appears on the left. A ferry is フェリー.
改 (examine, revise) + 札 (tag, ticket). Fully 改札口 'kaisatsuguchi'. Touch your IC card or insert the paper ticket; it is returned on the far side.
Clipped from English 'platform' (プラットホーム), so it also spells 'home'. 三番ホーム = platform 3. Mind the gap: 足元にご注意ください.
時刻 'jikoku' (point in time) + 表 (table). Japanese trains famously run to the printed minute; a delay certificate (遅延証明書) is issued if they are late.
急 (hurry) + 行 (go). Train grades on most lines: 各停 (every-stop local), 急行 (express), 特急 'tokkyū' (limited express, often extra fare). Check before boarding.
駐車 'chūsha' (parking) + 場 (place). 駐 shares the horse radical 馬 with 駅. Suffix 場 'jō' marks places: 工場 (factory), 会場 (venue).
片 (one of a pair) + 道 (road). Its opposite is 往復 'ōfuku' (round trip). The ticket machine asks 片道 or 往復.
往 (go) + 復 (return). 往復切符 = return ticket. Also 'back and forth': 往復する.

example.target: 往復でお願いします。

note: 出 (go out) + 口 (mouth, opening). Big stations have many: 東口 (east exit), 中央口 (central exit). Entrance is 入口 'iriguchi'.
今 (now) + 日 (day), with the special reading きょう. The formal reading こんにち is the one inside こんにちは.

example.target: 今日は暑いですね。
example.en: It is hot today, isn't it?

note: 明 (bright) + 日 (day): the next dawn. Casual reading あした; formal あす. 明後日 'asatte' = the day after tomorrow.
昨 (previous) + 日, read きのう. Formal reading さくじつ. 一昨日 'ototoi' = the day before yesterday.
いま; on reading こん in 今日, 今週 (this week), 今月 (this month). 今から = from now, 今すぐ = right now.
あさ; on reading ちょう in 朝食 'chōshoku' (breakfast). 今朝 'kesa' = this morning (irregular reading). 毎朝 = every morning.
ひる. 昼ご飯 = lunch, 昼休み 'hiruyasumi' = lunch break. お昼 is a common way to say 'lunch' itself.
よる; on reading や in 今夜 'kon'ya' (tonight) and 夜景 'yakei' (night view). Evening is 夕方 'yūgata'.

月 (moon) + 曜日 'yōbi' (weekday). The Japanese week follows the seven classical planets, just like the Romance languages: moon, fire (Mars), water (Mercury), wood (Jupiter), metal (Venus), earth (Saturn), sun.
火 (fire) stands for Mars, the fire planet (火星 'kasei'). Casual speech drops 日: 火曜.
水 (water) for Mercury, the water planet (水星). Note the on reading すい of 水, versus みず on its own.
木 (tree, wood) for Jupiter, the wood planet (木星). The reading もく is the on reading; き is the kun reading for a tree.
金 (metal, gold) for Venus, the metal planet (金星). The apostrophe in kin'yōbi separates ん from よ. 花金 'hanakin' once meant 'TGIF'.

example.target: 金曜日に映画を見ます。
example.en: I am going to see a film on Friday.

note: 土 (earth, soil) for Saturn, the earth planet (土星). 土日 'donichi' is shorthand for 'the weekend'.
日 (sun) + 曜日, so 日 appears twice with two readings: にち and び. Japanese calendars usually start the week on Sunday.
週 (week) + 末 (end). 週末に何をしますか = what are you doing at the weekend? 月末 'getsumatsu' and 年末 'nenmatsu' follow the same pattern.
来 (come) + 週 (week). The set: 先週 (last week), 今週 (this week), 来週 (next week); the same prefixes work with 月 (month) and 年 (year).

example.target: 来週、また会いましょう。

note: 先 (ahead, previous) + 月 (month, read げつ). 先 looks forward in space but backward in time, as in 先週 (last week). Next month is 来月 'raigetsu'.
毎 (every) + 日. The prefix works with any period: 毎朝 (every morning), 毎週 (every week), 毎年 'maitoshi' (every year).

example.target: 毎日日本語を勉強します。

note: 時 (hour) + 間 (interval). Means 'time' in general (時間がない, no time) and counts hours of duration: 二時間 'nijikan' = two hours, versus 二時 'niji' = two o'clock.
Reading changes with the number: 一分 'ippun', 二分 'nifun', 三分 'sanpun', 十分 'juppun'. The same kanji read わかる is the verb 'to understand' and read ぶん means 'portion'.
一時 'ichiji', 四時 'yoji' (not shiji), 七時 'shichiji', 九時 'kuji'. Add 半 for half past: 三時半 'sanjihan'. 何時 'nanji' = what time?

example.target: 七時に起きます。

note: Kun reading とし (year; also age); on reading ねん in 二〇二五年 (the year 2025) and 三年 (three years). 今年 'kotoshi' = this year, with an irregular reading.
一回 'ikkai' (once), 二回 'nikai', 三回 'sankai', 何回 'nankai' (how many times?). 週に二回 = twice a week. The kanji 回 also means 'to turn around'.
久しい 'hisashii' (long-lasting) + ぶり (after an interval of). As a greeting, お久しぶりです. Also an adverb: 久しぶりに会った = met for the first time in ages.
午 is the Horse of the zodiac, whose two-hour slot centered on noon, so 午前 is 'before noon' and 午後 'gogo' is after. 午前九時 = 9 a.m. Trains use the 24-hour clock.
いろ; on reading しょく in 景色 'keshiki' (scenery, irregular). Most color nouns end in 色: 黄色, 茶色, 水色. 色々 'iroiro' = various.

example.target: 何色が好きですか。

note: Noun form; the adjective is 赤い. 赤 appears in 赤ちゃん (baby) and 赤字 'akaji' (red ink, a deficit). The sun on the flag is officially 紅 'beni', crimson.
Historically 青 covered both blue and green, which survives in 青信号 (green traffic light), 青りんご (green apple) and 青葉 (fresh green leaves). Modern green is 緑.
黄 'ki' + 色. The adjective is 黄色い 'kiiroi'. One of only four basic colors with a true i-adjective (赤い, 青い, 白い, 黒い, plus 黄色い and 茶色い).
みどり. No i-adjective form: say 緑の 'midori no' (緑の車, a green car). Also means 'greenery'; 緑茶 'ryokucha' is green tea.
しろ; on reading はく in 白紙 (blank paper). 白黒 'shirokuro' = black and white; 紅白 'kōhaku' (red and white) is the festive color pair.
くろ; on reading こく in 黒板 'kokuban' (blackboard). 黒字 'kuroji' = in the black (profit).
茶 (tea) + 色: the color of brewed tea. Adjective 茶色い. Brown hair is 茶髪 'chapatsu'.
むらさき, named after the gromwell plant whose roots gave the dye. Once reserved for the highest court ranks. 紫式部 Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji.
English 'pink'. The native word is 桃色 'momoiro' (peach color); cherry blossom pink is 桜色 'sakurairo'.
English 'orange'; also the fruit. Native equivalent 橙色 'daidaiiro', after the bitter orange. Use with の: オレンジのシャツ.
灰 'hai' (ash) + 色. The loanword グレー 'gurē' is just as common, especially for clothes.
金 'kin' + 色. Gold leaf (金箔) covers Kyoto's 金閣寺 'Kinkakuji', the Golden Pavilion. Silver is 銀色 'gin'iro'.
銀 'gin' + 色. 銀 also appears in 銀行 (bank) and 銀座 'Ginza', once the site of the silver mint.
I-adjective from 赤. Goes directly before a noun: 赤い花 (a red flower). Negative 赤くない, past 赤かった.

example.target: 赤いかばんを買いました。

note: I-adjective. 青い空 (blue sky), 青い海. Also 'pale' (顔が青い) and 'green, unripe' of fruit or a person.
I-adjective. 白い雪 (white snow). 面白い 'omoshiroi' (interesting) literally contains 'white', though the connection is unclear.
I-adjective. 黒い猫 (a black cat). 腹黒い 'haraguroi' (black-bellied) = scheming.
かたち; on reading けい in 形容詞 'keiyōshi' (adjective). どんな形ですか = what shape is it?
まる. A circle ○ marks 'correct' on Japanese tests; a cross × (ばつ) marks 'wrong'. 丸い 'marui' = round. Ship names end in 丸.
三 (three) + 角 'kaku' (corner, angle). Onigiri are the classic 三角 shape. 三角形 'sankakkei' is the geometric term.
四 (four) + 角 (corner). 四角い 'shikakui' = square-shaped. Note the reading し here, not よん.
せん. Also a railway line: 山手線 'Yamanote-sen', 新幹線. The radical 糸 (thread) is on the left. 線を引く = to draw a line.
てん. Also a score or mark: 百点 'hyakuten' = full marks. The small dots on dakuten (゛) voice a kana: か → が.
水 (water) + 色: the pale blue of clear water. Japanese has many such nature colors: 桜色 (pink), 抹茶色 (matcha green), 空色 (sky blue).
からだ; on reading たい in 体育 'taiiku' (physical education) and 体温 (body temperature). 体に気をつけて = take care of yourself.
あたま. 頭がいい = clever ('head is good'). On reading とう in 先頭 (the front, the lead). Pitch accent: a-TA-ma.
かお. 顔を洗う = to wash one's face. 顔文字 'kaomoji' are the text faces like (^_^) that preceded emoji, itself a Japanese word: 絵 (picture) + 文字 (character).
め. The kanji is a turned eye pictograph. Also an ordinal suffix: 一つ目 'hitotsume' (the first), 二番目 (the second). 目薬 = eye drops.
みみ. Also the crust of bread (パンの耳). The radical appears in 聞く (to hear) and 聴く (to listen).
Homophone of 花 (flower), told apart by pitch: 鼻 'hana' is flat (hana-ga, LHH), 花 drops after the second mora (hana-ga, LHL). 鼻水 = runny nose.
くち. Also an opening or entrance: 入口, 出口, 窓口 'madoguchi' (service counter). On reading こう in 人口 'jinkō' (population).
て. Covers hand and often the arm. In compounds it means a person who does something: 歌手 'kashu' (singer), 選手 'senshu' (athlete), 運転手 (driver). 手紙 = letter.
あし, foot or whole leg (脚 is the stricter 'leg'). Also 'to add' as the verb 足す 'tasu' and 'sufficient' as 足りる 'tariru'. 足元 = at your feet.
お + 中 'naka' (middle), written with the body kanji 腹 'hara'. お腹が痛い = stomach ache, お腹がいっぱい = I'm full. Blunt 腹 is used mostly by men.

example.target: お腹がいっぱいです。

note: こころ: heart as feelings and spirit, not the organ (that is 心臓 'shinzō'). On reading しん in 安心 (relief), 心配 (worry). The kanji pictures a heart.
かみ, often 髪の毛 'kami no ke'. Homophones: 紙 (paper) and 神 (god). 髪を切る = to get a haircut. Body hair is 毛 'ke'.
は. 歯を磨く 'ha o migaku' = to brush teeth; 歯医者 'haisha' = dentist; 歯ブラシ = toothbrush.
病 (illness) + 気 (spirit, condition). 病気になる = to fall ill. The 気 of 元気 and 病気 is the same: your energy state.
風 (wind) + 邪 (evil), the old idea of a bad wind entering the body. You 'pull' a cold: 風邪をひく. Pitch tells it from 風 'kaze' (wind): 風邪 is KA-ze, 風 is ka-ZE.

example.target: 風邪をひきました。

note: ねつ. 熱がある = to have a fever. The same kanji gives 熱い 'atsui' (hot to the touch). Normal temperature is 平熱 'heinetsu'.
くすり; on reading やく in 薬局 (pharmacy). You 'drink' medicine in Japanese, even pills: 薬を飲む. The grass radical 艹 on top hints at herbal origins.

example.target: この薬を一日三回飲んでください。
example.roman: Kono kusuri o ichinichi sankai nonde kudasai.
example.en: Take this medicine three times a day.

note: 病 (illness) + 院 (institution). Also used for small clinics. Easily confused by learners with 美容院 'biyōin' (hair salon): short vowel び vs びょう.
医 (medicine) + 者 'sha' (person). Addressed as 先生. Polite form お医者さん. 歯医者 = dentist.
I-adjective, and the exclamation for 'ouch!'. Name the body part + が痛い: 頭が痛い (headache), 喉が痛い (sore throat). Slang 痛い also means cringe-worthy.
元 (origin, source) + 気 (spirit, energy). Na-adjective: 元気な子供. 元気です = I'm fine; 元気がない = looking down. 元気を出して = cheer up.
健 (robust) + 康 (peaceful, healthy). Na-adjective too: 健康な体. 健康診断 'kenkō shindan' = health check-up, an annual routine at Japanese companies.
Ru-verb. The past form 疲れた 'tsukareta' is how you say 'I'm tired' (the state resulting from getting tired). This is the verb inside お疲れ様.

example.target: 今日はとても疲れました。

note: 怪我 is ateji: the kanji 怪 (strange) and 我 (self) were chosen for sound. 怪我をする = to get injured. Often written in kana: けが.
The standard pattern for pain: body part + が + 痛い. Polite: 頭が痛いです. Also figurative: a headache-inducing problem.
Two kun readings: いえ (the building) and うち (one's home, family; also 'we'). On reading か in 家族 (family). 家に帰る = to go home.
部 (section) + 屋 (building), with the special reading へや. Rooms are measured in tatami mats: 六畳の部屋 = a six-mat room.
台 (stand, platform) + 所 (place). The modern word キッチン is equally common; 台所 sounds homely. 所 reads どころ here through rendaku.
Almost always with the honorific お. A deep tub for soaking, after washing outside it; the whole family shares the same hot water. お風呂に入る = take a bath.

example.target: お風呂に入ります。
example.en: I am going to take a bath.

note: Clipped from English 'toilet'. Polite alternatives: お手洗い 'otearai' (hand-washing place) and 化粧室 'keshōshitsu'. In homes the toilet is a separate room from the bath.

example.target: トイレはどこですか。

note: 玄 (dark, profound) + 関 (gate): originally the entrance to a Zen temple. The sunken area where you remove shoes before stepping up into the house.
English 'door', for Western hinged doors. A traditional sliding door is 戸 'to' or 引き戸; paper screens are 障子 'shōji' and 襖 'fusuma'.
まど. 窓を開ける = open the window. 窓口 'madoguchi' is a service counter (ticket window). 窓側 = window side (of a seat).
つくえ. The kanji has the tree radical 木 plus 几, a pictograph of a small table. A dining table is テーブル.
いす. The 子 suffix is a noun ending seen in 帽子 (hat) and 扇子 (fan). Traditional rooms have no chairs; you sit on 座布団 'zabuton' cushions.
English 'bed', with the small ッ doubling the d. Older spelling ベット is still seen. Japanese has no native word because people slept on futon.
Originally 蒲団, a round cushion of 蒲 (cattail rush); now 布 (cloth) + 団 (group, round). A mattress and quilt laid on tatami and folded away by day. Borrowed into English.
From 畳む 'tatamu' (to fold): originally thin mats that were folded up. Woven rush over rice straw, about 90 × 180 cm; room sizes are still given in mats (〜畳).
冷 (cold) + 蔵 (store) + 庫 (warehouse). A freezer is 冷凍庫 'reitōko' (freeze-warehouse). Both are usually 冷蔵庫 in casual talk.
Clipped from テレビジョン (television). Japanese loanwords are often cut to four morae: テレビ, パソコン, エアコン. テレビを見る = watch TV.
電 (electricity, lightning) + 気 (spirit, gas). Also means the room light: 電気をつける / 消す = turn the light on / off.

example.target: 電気を消してください。

note: Clipped from 'air conditioner'. In Japan the unit also heats, so it runs all year. クーラー 'kūrā' is an older word for the cooling function.
掃 (sweep) + 除 (remove) + する; irregular. 掃除機 'sōjiki' = vacuum cleaner. Japanese pupils clean their own classrooms (掃除の時間).

example.target: 週末に部屋を掃除します。
example.roman: Shūmatsu ni heya o sōji shimasu.
example.en: I clean my room at the weekend.

note: 洗 (wash) + 濯 (rinse) + する. 洗濯機 'sentakuki' = washing machine; 洗濯物 = the laundry. Most homes hang washing outside; dryers are rare.
かぎ; also 'lock'. 鍵をかける = to lock, 鍵を開ける = to unlock. The metal radical 金 is on the left.
にわ. 日本庭園 'nihon teien' is a formal Japanese garden. 家庭 'katei' (house + garden) means 'household, family life'.
かべ. Figurative too: 言葉の壁 = the language barrier. 壁紙 'kabegami' = wallpaper (and a screen wallpaper).
階 (floor, storey) + 段 (step). 階 also counts floors: 二階 'nikai' = second floor. Escalator is エスカレーター.
U-verb. The place takes に and the state uses te-iru: 東京に住んでいます = I live in Tokyo. 住所 'jūsho' = address. Not for 'to be alive', which is 生きる.

example.target: どこに住んでいますか。

note: A false friend: from English 'mansion', but it means a modern concrete apartment block, often owner-occupied. A cheaper wooden or two-storey building is an アパート.
ふく. 服を着る = to put on clothes. Also a counter for doses of medicine and the 服 of 制服 (uniform), 洋服 (Western clothes).
洋 (ocean; the West) + 服. Contrasts with 和服 'wafuku' (Japanese clothes). Since nearly everyone wears Western clothes, 洋服 just means 'clothes' in shops.
着 (wear) + 物 (thing): originally any clothing. Now the formal wrapped robe, worn at weddings, coming-of-age day and New Year. The word passed into English unchanged.
English 'shirt'; in Japan it can also mean an undershirt. A dress shirt is ワイシャツ 'waishatsu', from 'white shirt'.
Written with a Latin T plus katakana, a common hybrid in Japanese. Other such words: Yシャツ, Lサイズ, Eメール.
Usually traced to French 'jupon' (petticoat), though the origin is debated. Modern shops prefer パンツ 'pantsu', which however also means underpants.
English 'skirt'. The vowel u is inserted between s and k because Japanese syllables need a vowel; the long ā reflects the English 'ir'.
くつ. Removed at the door of homes, temples and some restaurants; 靴を脱ぐ = take off shoes. Counter 足 'soku': 一足 'issoku' = one pair.

example.target: ここで靴を脱いでください。
example.roman: Koko de kutsu o nuide kudasai.
example.en: Please take off your shoes here.

note: 靴 (shoe) + 下 (under): what goes under the shoe. Since shoes come off indoors, socks are on show; keep them hole-free. Traditional split-toe socks are 足袋 'tabi'.
ぼうし, with the noun suffix 子. You 'wear' a hat with the verb かぶる, not 着る: 帽子をかぶる.
English 'coat'; the same katakana also spells 'court' (テニスコート). Worn with the verb 着る.
上 (upper, read うわ) + 着 (wear). Any top layer: jacket, blazer, coat. 下着 'shitagi' (under-wear) is underwear.
下 'shita' (under) + 着 (wear, voiced to ぎ by rendaku). Covers underpants, bras and undershirts.
眼 (eye) + 鏡 (mirror), with the special reading めがね. Often in katakana メガネ on shop signs. 眼鏡をかける = to put on glasses (かける, to hang).
時 (time) + 計 (measure). Wristwatch 腕時計 'udedokei', alarm clock 目覚まし時計. Japan's Seiko and Citizen made the first quartz watches.
かさ. The kanji looks like an umbrella: a canopy over people. Cheap clear ビニール傘 are sold at every convenience store when rain starts.
Usually written in kana, かばん or カバン, since the kanji 鞄 is rare. Any bag you carry: briefcase, schoolbag, handbag. バッグ 'baggu' is the fashion word.
Ru-verb, for shirts, coats, dresses: anything on the torso. Its homophone 切る (to cut) is a u-verb: 着ます vs 切ります. Trousers and shoes use 履く, hats かぶる.

example.target: 今日は青いシャツを着ています。
example.roman: Kyō wa aoi shatsu o kite imasu.
example.en: I am wearing a blue shirt today.

en: to wear, put on (lower body: trousers, shoes)
note: U-verb for anything that goes on legs or feet: ズボンを履く, 靴を履く, 靴下を履く. Japanese splits 'wear' by body part: 着る (torso), 履く (legs), かぶる (head), かける (glasses).
U-verb; one verb covers all garments, unlike the many verbs for putting them on. Past 脱いだ, te-form 脱いで (ぐ verbs take だ/で). 靴を脱いでください = please remove your shoes.
English 'size'. Clothes use S, M, L, LL (not XL). Japanese sizes run small; shoe sizes are in centimetres: 26センチ.

example.target: もう少し大きいサイズはありますか。
example.roman: Mō sukoshi ōkii saizu wa arimasu ka.
example.en: Do you have a slightly bigger size?

note: English 'pocket'. ポケモン 'Pokemon' is ポケットモンスター (pocket monsters) clipped to four morae, a very Japanese way to shorten words.
English 'necktie'. Put on with the verb 締める 'shimeru' (to fasten): ネクタイを締める. Summer 'Cool Biz' lets office workers drop ties.
浴 (bathe) + 衣 (clothing), with a special reading. Originally worn after the bath; now the light cotton robe for summer festivals, fireworks and hot-spring inns, where one is provided.
制 (regulate, system) + 服. Most Japanese secondary schools require one; the sailor-style girls' uniform is セーラー服. Also for shop and company staff.
仕 (serve, do) + 事 'koto' (matter, thing), voiced to ごと. 仕事をする = to work. お仕事は何ですか = what do you do? Business talk: お仕事.

example.target: お仕事は何ですか。
example.en: What do you do for a living?

note: 会 (meet) + 社 (association, shrine). Reverse the kanji and you get 社会 'shakai' (society). 会社に行く = go to work; your own company is 弊社, the client's 御社.
会社 + 員 (member). The default answer to 'what do you do?'. The loan サラリーマン 'salaryman' is the informal word for a male office worker; women were called OL (office lady).
学 (learn) + 校 (school), with がく + こう contracting to がっこう. 小学校 (elementary), 中学校 (junior high), 高校 'kōkō' (high school).
大 (big) + 学 (learning), the title of a Confucian classic, The Great Learning. 大学生 = university student; 東大 'Tōdai' is short for 東京大学.
学 (learn) + 生 (life, person). Strictly a university student; school pupils are 生徒 'seito'. 留学生 'ryūgakusei' = international student.

example.target: 私は学生です。

note: 勉 (exert oneself) + 強 (strong, force): study is effort. Irregular suru-verb. In shops 勉強する can also mean 'to give a discount'.

example.target: 日本語を勉強しています。

note: 宿 (lodging, home) + 題 (problem, topic): problems taken home. 宿題をする = do homework. Also an unresolved issue left for later.
試 (try) + 験 (test, examine). 入学試験 = entrance exam; the JLPT is 日本語能力試験. テスト is used for small class tests.
授 (grant, impart) + 業 (work, trade). 授業を受ける = to take a class. 授業料 = tuition fees.
教 (teach) + 室 (room). Also a course or workshop: 料理教室 (cooking class), 英会話教室 (English conversation school).
The same kanji as in 日本 (origin of the sun, Japan) and the counter 〜本. Counter for books: 冊 'satsu'. 本屋 = bookshop.

example.target: 本を読むのが好きです。
example.roman: Hon o yomu no ga suki desu.

note: 鉛 (lead) + 筆 (brush), a Meiji-era coinage for a Western tool. Counted with 本. A mechanical pencil is シャープペンシル ('sharp pencil'), from a 1920s brand.
辞 (word) + 書 (writing, book). 電子辞書 'denshi jisho' (electronic dictionary) was the student standard before phones. Also 辞典 'jiten'.
From German 'Arbeit' (work), adopted by students in the Meiji era. Shortened to バイト. Not English 'part-time', which is パート, used for housewives' jobs.

example.target: コンビニでアルバイトをしています。
example.roman: Konbini de arubaito o shite imasu.
example.en: I work part-time at a convenience store.

note: 会 (meet) + 議 (discuss). 会議室 = meeting room, 会議中 = in a meeting. A casual team meeting is ミーティング.
給 (supply, provide) + 料 (fee, charge). 給料日 = payday, traditionally the 25th. Formal word on documents: 給与 'kyūyo'.
Noun from 休む 'yasumu' (to rest); the kanji shows a person 亻leaning on a tree 木. 夏休み = summer holidays, 昼休み = lunch break, お休み = closed (on shop signs).
U-verb. The kanji 働 (person 亻 + move 動) was invented in Japan; Chinese does not have it. 会社で働く = work at a company. 働き者 'hatarakimono' = hard worker.

example.target: 銀行で働いています。

note: Ru-verb. Also 'to tell, let know': 教えてください = please tell me (a name, the way). 教 is the kanji in 教室, 教師 (teacher) and 教会 (church).

example.target: 道を教えてください。

note: U-verb: to learn by taking lessons (ピアノを習う). Self-study is 勉強する; picking up a skill is 覚える. 習 shows wings 羽 over white 白: a fledgling practicing.
俳優 is the neutral word; 女優 'joyū' adds 女 (woman) for actress. 男優 'dan'yū' exists but is rarely used; a male actor is just 俳優.
社 (company) + 長 (chief, long). The suffix 長 marks the head of anything: 部長 (department head), 課長 (section chief), 校長 (school principal). Used as a title after the name.
残 (remain) + 業 (work). 残業する = to work overtime. A notorious feature of Japanese office life; 残業代 is overtime pay.
Clipped from パーソナルコンピューター (personal computer), taking the first two morae of each word. The same pattern gives スマホ (smartphone) and コンビニ.
天 (heaven, sky) + 気 (spirit, air). いい天気ですね (nice weather, isn't it) is the universal small talk. 天気予報 = weather forecast.

example.target: 今日はいい天気ですね。
example.roman: Kyō wa ii tenki desu ne.

note: Pitch-accent pair: 雨 'A-me' (high-low) is rain, 飴 'a-ME' (low-high) is candy. 雨が降る = it rains. June's rainy season is 梅雨 'tsuyu' (plum rain).
ゆき. The kanji has the rain radical 雨 on top, like 雲 (cloud) and 雷 (thunder). 雪が降る = it snows. 雪だるま = snowman ('snow Daruma').
かぜ, flat pitch (ka-ZE), versus 風邪 'KA-ze' (a cold). 風が強い = the wind is strong. On reading ふう in 和風 (Japanese-style) and 台風.
Noun from 晴れる 'hareru' (to clear up). Forecast words: 晴れ (sunny), 曇り (cloudy), 雨 (rain). 晴れ着 'haregi' = one's best clothes, for a 'bright' occasion.
From 曇る 'kumoru' (to cloud over). A cloud itself is 雲 'kumo', the same word as 蜘蛛 (spider), distinguished by pitch.
台 is used for its sound; 風 is wind. A cousin of English 'typhoon'. Typhoons are numbered, not named: 台風十号 = typhoon no. 10. Season: August to October.
地 (earth) + 震 (shake). Sounds like 自信 'jishin' (self-confidence). Japan has its own intensity scale, 震度 'shindo', from 0 to 7.
津 (harbor) + 波 (wave): the wave that devastates harbors. Adopted by English and now the international scientific term, replacing 'tidal wave'.
I-adjective for hot weather or air. Hot to the touch (tea, bath) is 熱い, same reading, different kanji. Japanese summers are 蒸し暑い 'mushiatsui' (steamy-hot).
I-adjective for cold weather or feeling cold. A cold object or drink is 冷たい 'tsumetai'. 寒い also describes a joke that falls flat.

example.target: 今朝は寒かったです。

note: I-adjective: pleasantly cool, as autumn air or shade. Its warm counterpart is 暖かい 'atatakai'. 涼しい顔 = a cool, unbothered face.
はる; on reading しゅん in 春分 (spring equinox). The school and fiscal year begin in April, with cherry blossom. 春休み = spring break.
なつ; on reading か in 夏季 (summer season). 夏休み = summer holidays; 夏祭り = summer festival, with yukata and fireworks (花火).
あき. The kanji combines rice 禾 and fire 火: harvest time. 紅葉 'kōyō' (autumn leaves) draws crowds like cherry blossom. 食欲の秋 = autumn, season of appetite.
ふゆ; on reading とう in 冬季 (winter season). 冬休み = winter break, around New Year. Snow country is 雪国 'yukiguni'.
やま; on reading さん in 富士山 'Fujisan' (Mount Fuji, not 'Fujiyama'). A pictograph of three peaks. Common in surnames: 山田, 山本.
かわ, a pictograph of flowing water. On reading せん in 河川 (rivers). Appended to names: 隅田川 'Sumidagawa' (with rendaku). Also a common surname element: 川口, 小川.
うみ; on reading かい in 海外 'kaigai' (overseas) and 北海道. 海の日 (Marine Day) is a July public holiday. 海辺 = seaside.

example.target: 夏は海に行きます。
example.en: In summer I go to the sea.

note: そら. The same kanji reads から 'empty' (空っぽ) and くう in 空港 (airport) and 空気 'kūki' (air). 青空 = blue sky.
き; on reading もく in 木曜日 (Thursday) and ぼく in 木材 (timber). A pictograph of a tree; doubled it is 林 (grove), tripled 森 (forest).
Homophone of 鼻 (nose); 花 has an accent drop after it (hana-ga, LHL), 鼻 is flat. 花見 'hanami' = blossom viewing; 花火 = fireworks (fire flowers). 生け花 = flower arranging.
さくら. Blooms for about a week from late March, tracked on the news as the 桜前線 (blossom front). 花見 parties are held under the trees. Also a girl's name.
いぬ; on reading けん in 柴犬 'shibaken' and 秋田犬. The kanji is a dog pictograph; as a radical it becomes 犭(犯, 猫). A dog says ワンワン.
ねこ. 招き猫 'manekineko' is the beckoning cat in shop windows. A cat says ニャー. 猫舌 'nekojita' (cat tongue) = someone who cannot eat hot food.

example.target: 猫を二匹飼っています。

note: お + 金 'kane' (metal, gold). The honorific お is almost always attached, so much that 'kane' alone sounds rough. 金 also reads きん (gold) and is Friday's kanji.
円 means 'circle, round'; the coins were round. English 'yen' keeps an old spelling 'ye'. Goes after the number: 百円 'hyakuen', 千円 'sen'en'. The ¥ sign is used in Japan too.
値 (value) + 段 (step, grade). 値段が高い / 安い = expensive / cheap. Price tags often show 税込 (tax included) and 税抜 (tax excluded) figures.
I-adjective with two senses: high/tall (背が高い, tall person) and expensive (値段が高い). The opposite for price is 安い, for height 低い 'hikui'.

example.target: ちょっと高いですね。

note: I-adjective. The kanji 安 also means 'peaceful, safe' (安心, 安全), so cheap and safe share a character. Attached to a verb, 〜やすい means 'easy to': 読みやすい.
みせ; on reading てん in 店員 (staff), 喫茶店. As a suffix shops take 屋 'ya': 本屋 (bookshop), パン屋 (bakery). お店 is the polite form.
Clipped from コンビニエンスストア (convenience store). Open 24 hours; sells meals, pays bills, has ATMs and prints documents. Seven-Eleven, Lawson and FamilyMart dominate.
Clipped from スーパーマーケット. Also means 'super' as a prefix. Discount stickers (半額, half price) appear on fresh food in the evening.
Clipped from 'department store'. The basement food hall is the デパ地下 'depachika', famous for gourmet take-away. Formal word: 百貨店 'hyakkaten' (hundred-goods shop).
U-verb ending in う: negative adds わ (買わない), te-form 買って. Homophone of 飼う (to keep a pet). 買い物 'kaimono' = shopping.

example.target: 新しい靴を買いたいです。
example.en: I want to buy new shoes.

note: U-verb. 売っています = is sold / they sell it. 売り切れ 'urikire' = sold out. The intransitive 売れる 'ureru' = to sell well.
U-verb. お金を払う = to pay money. Formal 支払う 'shiharau'. Also 'to brush off' dust, since paying was once 'clearing' a debt.

example.target: カードで払えますか。

note: 財 (wealth, property) + 布 (cloth). Japan is still coin-heavy, so wallets have big coin sections. 財布を忘れた = I forgot my wallet.
現 (present, actual) + 金 (money). 現金のみ = cash only, still common at small restaurants. Card payment: カード払い.
Clipped from レジスター (register). レジ袋 'reji-bukuro' = plastic shopping bag, charged for since 2020. Staff call レジへどうぞ when a till opens.
お + 釣り 'tsuri', from 釣る (to fish; to balance). Staff count it into your hand or a tray. Small change in general is 小銭 'kozeni'.
領 (receive) + 収 (collect) + 書 (document). The formal receipt for expense claims, with the company name written in; the ordinary till slip is レシート.
半 (half) + 分 (part). 半額 'hangaku' = half price. 半 alone follows times: 三時半 = half past three.
割 (divide) + 引 (pull, deduct), with rendaku. Discounts are stated in tenths: 二割引 'niwaribiki' = 20% off. 学割 'gakuwari' = student discount.
ふくろ. 袋はいりますか = do you need a bag? 紙袋 'kamibukuro' = paper bag; 福袋 'fukubukuro' = the sealed New Year lucky bag.

example.target: 袋はいりません。
example.en: I do not need a bag.

note: 無 (nothing) + 料 (fee). The opposite is 有料 'yūryō' (paid). Also written ただ in casual speech. 無料Wi-Fi is now common.
いくら (how much) + です + か. Point and ask これはいくらですか. Staff may show the figure on a calculator. Prices in Japan are rarely negotiable.

example.target: これはいくらですか。

note: 銀 (silver) + 行 (business house, a Chinese usage). Silver was the currency standard when the word was coined in the 19th century. 銀行員 = bank clerk.
お + 土産, read みやげ, a special reading unconnected to the kanji 土 (earth) 産 (product). Bringing edible gifts back from any trip, for colleagues and family, is a firm social duty.
両 (both; also an old coin) + 替 (exchange, voiced to がえ). Also means breaking a note into coins: 両替機 is the change machine in laundromats and arcades.
I-adjective for a momentary joy at something that happened (a gift, good news). Long-term happiness is 幸せ. Often in kana: うれしい.

example.target: 会えて嬉しいです。
example.en: I am happy to meet you.

note: I-adjective describing an enjoyable activity or time: 楽しかった = that was fun. The kanji 楽 also reads らく (easy, comfortable) and appears in 音楽 (music).

example.target: パーティーは楽しかったです。

note: I-adjective. The kanji 悲 has 心 (heart) at the bottom, like many feeling words: 悪, 思, 恋. 悲しみ 'kanashimi' = sadness (noun).
I-adjective meaning both 'frightening' (怖い映画, a scary film) and 'afraid' (怖いです, I'm scared). Learners confuse it with かわいい 'kawaii' (cute); the vowels differ.
I-adjective; also pronounced さみしい. Describes a person or a deserted, bleak place (寂しい道). The 寂 of 侘び寂び 'wabi-sabi', the beauty of quiet imperfection.
Na-adjective, not a verb: the liked thing takes が: 寿司が好きです = I like sushi. 好きな人 = the person I like. 大好き = love. From the verb 好く.

example.target: 日本の音楽が好きです。
example.roman: Nihon no ongaku ga suki desu.

note: Na-adjective despite ending in い: 嫌いな食べ物 (food I dislike), not 嫌いい. Quite strong; to be polite say あまり好きじゃない (I don't like it much).
大 (big) + 好き. Na-adjective: 大好きな歌 (a favorite song). The everyday way to say 'love' for food, hobbies and people; 愛している 'aishite iru' is dramatic.
Na-adjective and noun: 幸せな家族 (a happy family), 幸せになる (to become happy). The kanji 幸 also reads さち and こう in 幸運 (good luck).
I-adjective; also 'shy'. 恥 'haji' is shame. A very common reaction word, for praise as much as for mistakes.
心 (heart) + 配 (distribute, arrange): a heart spread thin. Na-adjective and suru-verb: 心配しないで = don't worry. 心配です = I'm worried.

example.target: 心配しないでください。

note: 安 (peaceful, safe) + 心 (heart). 安心する = to feel relieved; 安心してください = rest assured. The opposite of 心配.
U-verb. 怒っている = is angry (the state). The same kanji read いかる is literary 'to rage'. Not to be confused with 起こる 'okoru' (to happen), a homophone.

example.target: 母は怒っています。

note: U-verb covering both laughing and smiling (smile as a noun is 笑顔 'egao', laughing face). Online, 'w' and 草 (grass, from rows of w) stand for laughter.
U-verb. Its homophone 鳴く 'naku' is what animals do (a bird sings, a cat mews). 泣 has the water radical 氵for tears, 鳴 has a mouth 口 and bird 鳥.
U-verb; the cause takes に: 値段に驚いた = I was surprised at the price. Casual equivalent: びっくりする. The kanji 驚 has a horse 馬 at the bottom, a startled horse.
気 (spirit) + 持ち (holding). 気持ちいい = feels good (a breeze, a bath); 気持ち悪い = feels bad, gross. 気持ちは分かります = I understand how you feel.
I-adjective, from 眠る 'nemuru' (to sleep). 眠いです = I'm sleepy. 眠たい 'nemutai' is a variant. The kanji 眠 has the eye radical 目.
I-adjective covering both 'interesting' and 'amusing'. The kanji read 面 (face) + 白い (white); the origin of the expression is debated. Negative 面白くない = boring.

example.target: この本はとても面白いです。
example.roman: Kono hon wa totemo omoshiroi desu.

note: I-adjective in form, though it is really a negative verb (詰まらない, 'does not fill up'). Also 'trivial': つまらないものですが is the modest phrase when handing over a gift.
残 (remain) + 念 (thought, feeling): a feeling that lingers. Na-adjective: 残念です = that's a pity; 残念ながら = unfortunately.

example.target: 行けなくて残念です。
example.en: It is a pity I cannot go.

en: to be troubled, in a fix
note: U-verb. 困っています = I'm in trouble / stuck, the phrase to use when you need help. 困った人 = a difficult person. 困ります = that would be a problem (a polite refusal).

example.target: 道が分からなくて困っています。
example.en: I am stuck because I don't know the way.

note: 緊 (tight) + 張 (stretch): strung taut. Irregular suru-verb. 緊張しています = I'm nervous, before an exam or speech. Also 'tension' between countries.
Noun from 楽しむ 'tanoshimu' (to enjoy). 楽しみです = I'm looking forward to it; 楽しみにしています is the polite version used in emails.
U-verb; the thought is quoted with と: 面白いと思います = I think it's interesting. For reasoning or pondering, use 考える 'kangaeru'. 思い出 'omoide' = memories.

example.target: いいと思います。

note: U-verb with one irregularity: the past and te-form are 行った, 行って (not 行いた). The destination takes に or へ: 学校に行く. On reading こう in 旅行, 銀行.

example.target: 明日、東京に行きます。
example.en: I am going to Tokyo tomorrow.

note: One of only two truly irregular verbs (with する): the kanji 来 stays but its reading changes: 来ます 'kimasu', 来ない 'konai', 来た 'kita'. Compare 来週, 来月 (next week, next month).

example.target: 友達が日本に来ます。
example.en: My friend is coming to Japan.

note: Irregular verb, and the engine of the language: noun + する makes a verb (勉強する, 電話する, 運転する). Its potential form is a separate verb, できる 'dekiru' (can do).

example.target: 週末は何をしますか。
example.roman: Shūmatsu wa nani o shimasu ka.
example.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

note: Ru-verb. Covers see, look and watch: テレビを見る, 映画を見る. After a te-form, 〜てみる means 'try doing': 食べてみる = try eating. 見せる 'miseru' = to show.

example.target: 昨日、映画を見ました。

note: U-verb with two meanings: to hear/listen (音楽を聞く) and to ask (先生に聞く). For 'listen attentively' some write 聴く. The kanji is an ear 耳 inside a gate 門.

example.target: ちょっと聞いてもいいですか。
example.roman: Chotto kiite mo ii desu ka.

note: U-verb; す verbs take した/して. 日本語を話す = speak Japanese. The noun 話 'hanashi' (a talk, story) drops the す. Homophone 離す = to separate.

example.target: 英語を話せますか。

note: U-verb; む verbs take んだ/んで. 本を読む = read a book. 読み方 'yomikata' = the reading of a kanji. 空気を読む (read the air) = sense the mood.

example.target: 漢字が読めません。

note: U-verb; く verbs take いた/いて. Homophone 描く 'kaku' = to draw. The radical 聿 is a hand holding a brush; 書 also means 'book, document' (辞書, 領収書).

example.target: ここに名前を書いてください。
example.roman: Koko ni namae o kaite kudasai.

note: Ru-verb: going to bed and lying down; being asleep is 眠る 'nemuru'. 寝ます 'nemasu'. 寝坊 'nebō' = oversleeping; 昼寝 = a nap.

example.target: 毎晩十一時に寝ます。
example.en: I go to bed at eleven every night.

note: Ru-verb: 起きます 'okimasu'. Also 'to happen' (事故が起きる, an accident occurs). The transitive 起こす 'okosu' = to wake someone up.

example.target: 何時に起きますか。
example.en: What time do you get up?

note: U-verb for making anything: 料理を作る (cook), 友達を作る (make friends). 手作り 'tezukuri' = handmade. On reading さく in 作品 (a work) and 作家 (writer).

example.target: 晩ご飯を作ります。

note: U-verb; the person you meet takes に, not を: 友達に会う. Te-form 会って. The kanji 会 is the one in 会社 and 会議. Homophone 合う = to fit, match.

example.target: 駅で友達に会いました。
example.en: I met a friend at the station.

note: U-verb; つ verbs take った/って. ちょっと待って = wait a moment; polite 少々お待ちください. Homophone 松 'matsu' = pine tree.

example.target: ここで待っていてください。

note: A trap: it ends in -eru but is a u-verb: 帰ります, 帰って (not 帰て). Means returning to where you belong (home, your country). Homophones: 変える (change), 蛙 (frog).

example.target: そろそろ帰ります。
example.en: I should be heading home soon.

en: to go out, leave; to appear
note: Ru-verb; the place you leave takes を: 家を出る. Also 'to come out, appear' (テレビに出る, be on TV) and 'to answer the phone' (電話に出る). Transitive 出す 'dasu' = take out.
Another -iru verb that is a u-verb: 入ります, 入って. The place takes に: お風呂に入る (take a bath), 大学に入る (enter university). Transitive 入れる 'ireru' = put in.

example.target: 入ってもいいですか。

note: U-verb. お箸を使う = use chopsticks; お金を使う = spend money. 使い方 'tsukaikata' = how to use. The kanji is in 大使館 (embassy, 'great envoy hall').

example.target: これを使ってもいいですか。
example.roman: Kore o tsukatte mo ii desu ka.

note: U-verb. 持っています = I have (own) it; 持って行く = take along; 持って来る = bring. 気持ち and 持ち帰り contain its stem 持ち.

example.target: 傘を持っていますか。

note: U-verb; the seat takes に: 椅子に座る. Polite invitation: どうぞお座りください or お掛けください. 正座 'seiza' is the formal kneeling sit on tatami.
U-verb; ぶ verbs take んだ/んで. Not for sports or instruments (those use する and 弾く); 遊ぶ is hanging out, visiting, kids playing. 遊びに来てください = come and visit.
Ru-verb, transitive: 窓を開ける (open the window). The intransitive pair 開く 'aku' = to open (by itself): ドアが開く. 閉める 'shimeru' = to close.

example.target: 窓を開けてもいいですか。
example.roman: Mado o akete mo ii desu ka.

note: Ru-verb: to commit to memory (漢字を覚える). 覚えています = I remember (the state). For recalling something you had forgotten, use 思い出す 'omoidasu'.
Ru-verb. 忘れました = I forgot; 忘れ物 'wasuremono' = something left behind (announced constantly on trains). The kanji 忘 is 亡 (perish) over 心 (heart).

example.target: パスワードを忘れました。

note: U-verb; the thing understood takes が, not を: 日本語が分かります. 分かりました = understood / will do. The kanji 分 (divide) is also 'minute' and 'portion'.

example.target: すみません、よく分かりません。

note: U-verb, pronounced ゆう in speech though written いう. What is said is quoted with と: 「はい」と言った. 〜と言います = is called: 田中と言います (my name is Tanaka).

example.target: もう一度言ってください。

note: なに on its own; なん before d, t, n and counters: 何ですか 'nan desu ka', 何時 'nanji', 何人 'nannin'. 何か 'nanika' = something; 何も + negative = nothing.

example.target: これは何ですか。

note: だれ. Polite form どなた 'donata'. 誰か = someone, 誰も + negative = no one. 誰の = whose.

example.target: あの人は誰ですか。
example.roman: Ano hito wa dare desu ka.

note: One of the ko-so-a-do series: ここ (here), そこ (there, by you), あそこ (over there), どこ (where). Polite: どちら. 出身はどこですか = where are you from?

example.target: 駅はどこですか。

note: No particle needed: いつ来ますか = when are you coming? いつも = always, いつか = someday, いつでも = anytime. Not to be confused with 五つ 'itsutsu' (five).
Slightly formal; in conversation どうして 'dōshite' and casual なんで 'nande' are more common. Answers end in から (because): 忙しいからです.
どうですか = how is it / how about it? Polite いかが. どうやって = how (by what method); どうして = why. Part of どうぞ, どうも, どういたしまして.

example.target: 日本はどうですか。

note: Stands alone: どれがいいですか = which one is good? Before a noun use どの: どの電車. For a choice of two, どちら 'dochira' (also 'which direction', and polite 'where').
Goes before a noun: どんな人 (what kind of person), どんな音楽 (what kind of music). Series: こんな (this kind), そんな, あんな, どんな.

example.target: どんな食べ物が好きですか。
example.roman: Donna tabemono ga suki desu ka.
example.en: What kind of food do you like?

note: Near the speaker. Stands alone as a noun; before a noun use この: この本 (this book). Series: これ, それ (near listener), あれ (far from both), どれ (which).
Near the listener, or just mentioned. それは何ですか = what is that (you have)? Something far from both speakers is あれ 'are'. Before a noun: その, あの.
ここ (here), そこ (there), あそこ (over there), どこ (where). ここです = it's here. On a map: 現在地 'genzaichi' = you are here.
Used far less than English 'you': Japanese prefer the person's name + さん or just omit it. Addressing a superior as あなた can sound rude. Wives also use it for 'dear' to husbands.
Marks the topic of the sentence: 私は学生です (as for me, I'm a student). Written with the kana は (ha) but pronounced 'wa', a spelling kept from old Japanese. Contrast with が.
Marks the grammatical subject, especially new or emphasized information and the thing with 好き, 分かる, ある: 猫がいます (there is a cat). Question words always take が, never は: 誰が来ますか.
Marks the direct object: パンを食べる. Pronounced 'o', identical to お; the kana を survives almost only as this particle. Also marks the place you move through or leave: 公園を歩く.
Links nouns: 私の本 (my book), 日本の車 (Japanese cars), 東京の駅 (a station in Tokyo). Also a pronoun 'one': 赤いの = the red one. One of the most frequent words in Japanese.

example.target: これは私の傘です。
example.roman: Kore wa watashi no kasa desu.

en: to, at, in (direction, time, location of existence)
note: Destination (東京に行く), time (三時に), location where something exists (家にいる), and indirect object (友達に会う). Compare で, which marks where an action happens.
Marks where an action takes place (学校で勉強する) and the means or tool (電車で行く, 日本語で話す). Also 'because of' and the te-form of です.

example.target: レストランで晩ご飯を食べました。
example.en: I had dinner at a restaurant.

note: Turns a sentence into a question with no change of word order: 学生です → 学生ですか. Written questions often omit the ? mark. Between nouns it means 'or': コーヒーか紅茶.
Replaces は or が: 私も学生です (I am also a student). With question words and a negative it means 'no-': 誰もいない (nobody is there), 何もない (there is nothing).

example.target: 私もコーヒーをお願いします。
example.roman: Watashi mo kōhī o onegai shimasu.

note: Starts a sentence: でも、高いです (but it's expensive). After a noun it means 'even' or 'or something': お茶でも飲みませんか (how about tea or something?).
Goes before adjectives: とても美味しい. Casual alternatives すごく 'sugoku' and めっちゃ 'meccha' (Kansai, now nationwide). With a negative, とても means 'not possibly'.
'A bit' (ちょっと高い), 'a moment' (ちょっと待って), and a soft 'no': it's a bit... (ちょっと...). Also used to get attention: ちょっとすみません.

example.target: 今日はちょっと忙しいです。

en: to exist, there is (things); to have
note: For inanimate things and plants; living beings use いる. Irregular negative ない (not あらない). 時間があります = I have time. Usually in kana; the kanji 有る / 在る are rare.

example.target: 近くにコンビニがありますか。
example.roman: Chikaku ni konbini ga arimasu ka.
example.en: Is there a convenience store nearby?

note: For people and animals; things use ある. Ru-verb: います, いない. Also the auxiliary in 〜ている (is doing): 食べている. Homophones 要る (need, a u-verb) and 入る.

example.target: 兄弟がいますか。

note: I-adjective. Note the long ō spelled おお (not おう). Before a noun 大きな is also used: 大きな木. The kanji 大 pictures a person with arms spread wide.
I-adjective; 小さな also appears before nouns. 小 is the kanji in 小学校 (elementary school) and 小さい子 (small child). Opposite: 大きい.

example.target: この部屋は小さいです。

note: I-adjective. On reading しん in 新聞 'shinbun' (newspaper), 新幹線, 新年 (New Year). Fresh fish or vegetables are also 新しい or 新鮮 'shinsen'.
I-adjective for objects and ideas, never for people (an old person is 年を取った or お年寄り). 古本 'furuhon' = second-hand books; 中古 = used (cars, goods).
Irregular i-adjective: other forms come from よい: past よかった 'yokatta', negative よくない. いいですよ = sure, go ahead; いいです can also mean 'no thanks', so watch the tone.

example.target: それはいい考えですね。
example.roman: Sore wa ii kangae desu ne.

note: I-adjective. 悪い! on its own is a casual 'my bad, sorry' (mostly male). 気持ち悪い = gross, sick-feeling. The kanji has 心 (heart) at the bottom.
I-adjective, for length and time (長い間, a long while). On reading ちょう in 社長, 部長: the 'chief' is the 'long' one, i.e. the senior.
I-adjective, for length and time; a short person is 背が低い, not 短い. The kanji 短 shows an arrow 矢 and a bean 豆, two short things.
I-adjective, same sound as 速い (fast) but a different kanji: 早い is about time (early in the morning, too soon), 速い about speed. 早く = early / quickly, hurry up!

example.target: 朝早く起きました。
example.en: I got up early in the morning.

note: I-adjective for speed: 新幹線は速い. Its homophone 早い means early. The kanji 速 appears in 速度 'sokudo' (speed) and 高速道路 (expressway).
I-adjective covering both late (もう遅い, it's already late) and slow (歩くのが遅い). The verb 遅れる 'okureru' = to be late. 遅刻 'chikoku' = lateness.
I-adjective for rooms, roads and areas: 広い部屋 (a spacious room). Also 'broad' (知識が広い). The common name 広島 Hiroshima means 'wide island'.
I-adjective; the opposite of 広い. 狭い部屋 (a cramped room). Tokyo apartments are famously 狭い. 肩身が狭い = feeling small, ashamed.
I-adjective. Also serious (重い病気, a serious illness). Opposite 軽い 'karui' (light). The kanji 重 also means 'to pile up', as in 重ねる.

example.target: この荷物は重いです。

note: I-adjective for people, wind, drinks and teams: お酒に強い = can hold one's drink. Opposite 弱い 'yowai'. On reading きょう in 勉強 and 強い風 (strong wind).
I-adjective: bright light or color, and a cheerful personality (明るい人). The kanji 明 joins sun 日 and moon 月, and is in 明日 (tomorrow).
I-adjective: dark (暗い部屋) and gloomy in personality. Opposite of 明るい. Not to be confused with the particle くらい/ぐらい (about, approximately).
Na-adjective: 静かな町 (a quiet town), 静かです. 静かにしてください = please be quiet. The 静 of 静岡 Shizuoka.

example.target: この公園はとても静かです。
example.roman: Kono kōen wa totemo shizuka desu.

note: Na-adjective: 賑やかな街 (a bustling street). Positive in tone, unlike うるさい (noisy, annoying). Usually written にぎやか; the kanji 賑 is hard.
Na-adjective despite its final い: 綺麗な花, negative 綺麗じゃない (never 綺麗くない). Means both beautiful and clean. Almost always written きれい or キレイ.

example.target: 桜がとても綺麗ですね。
example.roman: Sakura ga totemo kirei desu ne.
example.en: The cherry blossoms are very beautiful.

note: 有 (have) + 名 (name). Na-adjective: 有名な人 (a famous person). 〜で有名 = famous for: 京都はお寺で有名です.
便 (convenience) + 利 (benefit). Na-adjective; the Japanese word of praise for gadgets, apps and locations: 駅が近くて便利です. Opposite 不便 'fuben'.
簡 (simple) + 単 (single). Na-adjective: 簡単な問題 (an easy question). For 'easy to do' there is also 易しい 'yasashii', homophone of 優しい (kind).
I-adjective. 難しいですね in a negotiation is often a soft 'no'. The kanji 難 is in 災難 (disaster) and 難民 (refugees). Opposite: 易しい or 簡単.

example.target: 漢字は難しいですが、面白いです。
example.roman: Kanji wa muzukashii desu ga, omoshiroi desu.

note: I-adjective. The kanji 忙 is 忄(heart) + 亡 (perish): the heart lost in busyness. お忙しいところすみません = sorry to bother you when you're busy.
まち; on reading ちょう in addresses (〜町). The rice-field radical 田 on the left. 街, also まち, is a street or downtown area: 街に行く = go into town.
東 (east) + 京 (capital), named in 1868 when the emperor moved from Kyoto. Both vowels are long: とうきょう. Greater Tokyo is the largest metropolitan area in the world.
日 (sun) + 本 (origin): the land where the sun rises, as seen from China. Two readings: にほん (everyday) and にっぽん (formal, on stamps and at sports events). 日本語 = Japanese language.

example.target: 日本は初めてですか。
example.en: Is this your first time in Japan?

note: 公 (public) + 園 (garden). Also 国立公園 (national park). Sounds like 講演 'kōen' (lecture); context decides.
図書 (books) + 館 (hall, large building). The suffix 館 'kan' marks public buildings: 映画館, 美術館, 大使館, 旅館.
郵便 'yūbin' (mail) + 局 (bureau, office). Marked by the symbol 〒, also used before postcodes. Post offices double as banks (ゆうちょ銀行).
交 (alternate) + 番 (turn, watch): officers originally took turns standing guard. Small neighborhood police posts; ask here for directions or lost property. The word is now used in English.
神 (god, kami) + 社 (shrine, association). Recognized by the torii gate; visitors bow, throw a coin, clap twice and bow. A Buddhist temple is お寺.
寺 'tera' with the honorific お; in temple names the kanji reads じ: 清水寺 'Kiyomizu-dera', 金閣寺 'Kinkakuji'. Temples have statues and incense; shrines have torii.
映画 'eiga' (film: 映 project + 画 picture) + 館 (hall). 映画を見に行く = go to see a film. Foreign films come as 字幕 (subtitled) or 吹き替え (dubbed).
美術 'bijutsu' (fine art: 美 beauty + 術 technique) + 館. A history or science museum is 博物館 'hakubutsukan'.
The classic pitch-accent example: 橋 'haSHI' (low-high, falling after) is bridge, 箸 'HAshi' (high-low) is chopsticks, 端 'hashi' (flat) is edge. In place names it is voiced: 日本橋 'Nihonbashi'.
建て 'tate' (stem of 建てる, to build) + 物 (thing). Any structure; a tall office block is ビル.
Clipped from ビルディング 'building'. Short vowel: ビル (building) vs ビール (beer). Floors are counted with 階: 五階建てのビル = a five-storey building.
入り 'iri' (entering) + 口 (mouth, opening). Its partner 出口 'deguchi' is exit. Also written 入り口. 非常口 'hijōguchi' = emergency exit.
From 通る 'tōru' (to pass through). Named streets end in it: 表参道 Omotesandō, 中央通り (Central Avenue). Also 'as': その通り = exactly so.
場 (place, ground) + 所 (place), two near-synonyms doubled. Also a sumo tournament (one of six 場所 a year). いい場所 = a good spot.

example.target: この場所はどこですか。
example.roman: Kono basho wa doko desu ka.

note: くに; on reading こく in 外国 (foreign country), 中国 (China), 国際 (international). お国はどちらですか = which country are you from? (polite).
外 (outside) + 国 (country). 外国人 'gaikokujin' = foreigner, shortened to 外人 'gaijin', which some find rude. 外国語 = foreign language.
田 (rice field) + 舎 (hut), read いなか, a reading not derived from either kanji. Means both rural areas and one's rural hometown: 田舎に帰る = go back home to the country.
市 (city) + 役所 'yakusho' (government office). Where residents register addresses and get certificates. A ward office in big cities is 区役所 'kuyakusho'.
本 (book) + 屋 'ya' (shop, house). The suffix 屋 names most small shops: 花屋 (florist), 魚屋 (fishmonger), 八百屋 (greengrocer), and also people: 頑張り屋 (hard worker).
動物 'dōbutsu' (animal: 動 move + 物 thing) + 園 (garden). Ueno Zoo in Tokyo, founded 1882, is Japan's oldest. An aquarium is 水族館 (water-family hall).
京 (capital) + 都 (metropolis). Japan's capital for over a thousand years, until 1868. The first vowel is long: きょうと. 京 is also the きょう of 東京.
となり. 駅の隣 = next to the station; 隣の人 = the person next door, or in the next seat. Position words: 前 (front), 後ろ (behind), 上 (above), 下 (below), 中 (inside).

example.target: 銀行は郵便局の隣です。
example.roman: Ginkō wa yūbinkyoku no tonari desu.
example.en: The bank is next to the post office.
